localBiteReport: Note: The most current sourced reports are from late July 2026 (roughly two weeks old), as no posts dated this week (Aug 1–5) were found. That said, conditions in the bay appear active. A Santa Rosa Beach guide reporting about six days ago (approximately July 30) noted a strong speckled trout bite with good numbers and quality fish, plus a notable bull redfish catch — a 40¼-inch, 26-lb fish landed in the bay. Water temp is 85°F at this location. FishingBooker's July Choctawhatchee Bay overview similarly highlights bull redfish and trophy-class trout as the headline inshore targets, with guides recommending early-morning departures to beat summer heat and crowds. The Half Hitch Destin report from July 20 (the most recent retrievable post) focused largely on offshore action, but bay trout had been described as consistent and scattered throughout the system in the weeks prior, with anglers finding fish by being selective about wind-sheltered areas.

aiSummary: Choctawhatchee Bay is fishing well this week with the most recent reports — from around July 30 — describing a strong speckled trout bite with good numbers and quality fish, plus bull redfish showing in the bay, including a notable 40¼-inch, 26-lb fish. Today's conditions feature light WSW winds under 10 mph, 85°F water, and slightly stained clarity, all favorable for an early push on protected grass flats and oyster bars. Plan to be on the water at first light and off before midday — a 29% storm chance with a window before 4 PM and a high of 91°F make the morning hours both the safest and most productive window.

bridge.aiNote: The 331 Bridge spans the narrow neck of Choctawhatchee Bay, creating a current funnel that pushes bait through on both tides and concentrates trout, redfish, sheepshead, and black drum around the pilings year-round. Lee-side pilings are the prime ambush zone on incoming tides. Being open and exposed, this is the first spot on the bay to become unfishable when wind picks up or weather builds.
bridge.todaysCall: Low tide hits around 10:15 AM, so the incoming tide through the afternoon creates the current push that makes the bridge pilings most productive — target the lee-side pilings as water starts moving back up. Light WSW winds under 10 mph through the morning should keep chop manageable, but the bridge's exposed open-water character means any afternoon storm development will make conditions deteriorate fast. With storms possible before 4 PM, plan to fish the early morning window at sunrise (6:04 AM) on the outgoing tide, then reassess before committing to a midday session. Slightly stained water favors noisy or chartreuse soft plastics worked along the pilings for trout and reds.

alaqua.aiNote: Alaqua Bayou offers well-protected water with a strong year-round redfish population, plus trout and flounder near the mouth. The oyster bars at the creek mouth are the prime holding structure. Tree cover keeps temperatures a few degrees cooler than the open bay and provides meaningful shelter from wind and weather, making it a reliable option when conditions build.
alaqua.todaysCall: With water temps at 85°F across the bay, Alaqua's tree-shaded interior is a smart play today — that natural cooling effect can make a real difference in fish activity and comfort during a hot August morning. Fish the oyster bars at the creek mouth on the outgoing tide before the 10:15 AM low, then probe the upper creek edges as the tide begins to fill back in. Light WSW winds won't affect this protected water much, and the slightly stained clarity calls for darker or rattling lures to help reds locate the bait. Get here early and be off the water or under cover before the pre-4 PM storm window opens.

basin.aiNote: Basin Bayou sees less pressure than nearby Alaqua and LaGrange, which generally means less-educated fish willing to bite. The interior grass flats are classic sight-fishing water for redfish in under two feet, and pompano occasionally show at the mouth on moving tides. It offers less weather protection than LaGrange when conditions deteriorate.
basin.todaysCall: The light-pressure fishery here is worth the trip on a calm morning like this one — WSW winds under 10 mph won't push much chop into the bayou, and the slightly stained water on the shallow grass flats should still allow sight-fishing for reds if you're moving slowly. Focus the outgoing tide on interior grass flats before the 10:15 AM low, looking for tailing or pushing fish in under two feet. With afternoon storms possible before 4 PM and Basin offering less weather protection than LaGrange, commit to an early start at or just after sunrise (6:04 AM) and plan your exit before noon. If you draw a blank on reds inside, check the bayou mouth on the incoming tide for any pompano straggling into summer.

lagrange.aiNote: LaGrange Bayou is the top trout producer on this dashboard, with legendary oyster bars at the mouth and interior grass flats that hold redfish year-round. Deep holes inside also hold black drum and sheepshead. It is the most protected water on this side of the bay, making it the default go-to when weather threatens.
lagrange.todaysCall: With a strong trout bite documented across the bay in late July and LaGrange consistently ranked as the top local trout producer, today's morning session here should be a high-confidence move. Fish the oyster bars at the mouth on the outgoing tide leading into the 10:15 AM low, then transition to the interior grass flats for reds as the tide turns and starts pushing back in. Light WSW winds under 10 mph will barely register in this protected water, and slightly stained clarity actually suits an oyster-bar bite well — reds and trout key in on sound and vibration in off-color water, so rattling corks or paddle tails with some noise are good choices. LaGrange's protected character means you have more flexibility to stay through a midday storm threat than almost anywhere else on the bay, but the pre-4 PM window is still the safer and more productive half of the day.

fourmile.aiNote: Four Mile Creek is a short tidal creek running between Shipyard Marina and the bay, where incoming tides push baitfish up the creek and concentrate redfish and trout in the bends and grass edges. The creek mouth is a reliable flounder zone, and the upper section transitions to brackish water holding bass and small reds. It is the most protected fishery in this part of the bay when weather threatens.
fourmile.todaysCall: Four Mile is a smart pick today if you want a short run and a built-in weather shelter — its compact, protected nature means afternoon storm risk is less of a factor here than anywhere else on the dashboard. Fish the outgoing tide through the bends and grass edges before the 10:15 AM low, then position yourself at the creek mouth as the tide turns to intercept flounder and any trout staging to feed on the incoming push. Light WSW winds won't penetrate the creek at all. Slightly stained water calls for slower, bottom-hugging presentations for flounder at the mouth — a scented soft plastic on a light jig head worked along the edges is hard to beat in these conditions.

hogtown.aiNote: Hogtown Bayou is a signature Santa Rosa Beach guide spot and one of the most productive trout flats on the bay, with summer mornings peak for trout stacked on grass in two to four feet of water. Spanish mackerel show at the mouth on moving tides. It sees regular pressure but produces consistently, and its greater distance from the 331 Bridge means run time is a real factor to build into your plan.
hogtown.todaysCall: The late-July guide report of a strong speckled trout bite with good numbers and quality fish originated from a Santa Rosa Beach guide — Hogtown is that guide's signature spot, making it directly relevant here. An early start is especially important: guides have been recommending morning departures to beat summer heat, and with the high at 91°F and storm risk before 4 PM, hitting the grass flats at or just after sunrise (6:04 AM) is the play. Target the two-to-four-foot grass zone on the outgoing tide before the 10:15 AM low, working topwaters or weedless soft plastics in the slightly stained water. Factor in the longer run time from the 331 area — leave early enough that you're already fishing by first light, not still on plane.

mallet.aiNote: Mallet Bayou is a small tributary feeding directly into LaGrange Bayou, just south of Freeport. Its direct connection to LaGrange — the top trout producer on this dashboard — suggests the oyster-bar trout-and-redfish pattern from the larger bayou can plausibly extend into this quieter water. There is far less documented fishing history for Mallet Bayou itself, but its small, interior character makes it a natural calm-water fallback when wind picks up on the open bay.
mallet.todaysCall: Today's light winds and manageable conditions don't force anyone to hide in the smallest water, but Mallet's direct connection to LaGrange makes it worth a look if you want to explore a less-pressured extension of that productive system. Fish it on the same outgoing-tide window as LaGrange — before the 10:15 AM low — working any oyster structure or grass edges you find inside. Slightly stained water is typical for interior bayous and shouldn't be a deterrent; use lures with some noise or scent to help fish locate them. Treat this as a secondary stop on a LaGrange-focused trip rather than a standalone destination, given the limited fishing history here.

mack.aiNote: Mack Bayou sits on the barrier-island (30-A) side of Choctawhatchee Bay near Topsail Hill Preserve State Park, well west of the 331 Bridge — a long-run destination that requires deliberate planning. It shares protected-bayou character with Alaqua and LaGrange, featuring marsh grass, oyster bars, and interior holes, with lighter pressure simply due to its distance from the main ramps. Hewett and Buck Bayou sit immediately to the east and are realistically fishable in the same trip.
mack.todaysCall: The long run to Mack Bayou demands an early departure today — leave before sunrise (6:04 AM) to reach this 30-A-side spot and have meaningful fishing time before midday heat and the pre-4 PM storm window close in. Light WSW winds under 10 mph are favorable for the run across the open bay and won't create difficult conditions inside the bayou itself. Work the oyster bars and grass edges on the outgoing tide before the 10:15 AM low, then decide whether to push into Hewett Bayou next door before heading back. The lower pressure at this distance often means less-spooked fish — the extra run time can pay off on a calm, fishable morning like this one.

hewett.aiNote: Hewett Bayou sits immediately east of Mack Bayou on the barrier-island (30-A) side of Choctawhatchee Bay, near Topsail Hill Preserve State Park, and pairs naturally with Mack and Buck Bayou in a single trip. It features the same protected-bayou habitat — oyster bars and marsh grass at the mouth, deeper interior holes further in. Light pressure due to its distance from the main boat ramps makes this a consistently underrated option.
hewett.todaysCall: Like Mack Bayou next door, Hewett rewards anglers willing to make the long run — and today's light WSW winds under 10 mph make that run as comfortable as it gets in August. Plan Hewett as the second stop on a Mack-Hewett morning, working the mouth structure and grass edges on the outgoing tide before the 10:15 AM low, then probing the interior holes for trout or reds as the tide turns. Slightly stained clarity is consistent with what you'd expect in a bayou of this type; a slow-sinking soft plastic or gold spoon along the oyster-bar edges is a reliable approach. Turn for home well before the pre-4 PM storm window — the long return run across open water is not where you want to be when thunderstorms fire up.

buck.aiNote: Buck Bayou is the smallest and least-documented of the three neighboring bayous on the barrier-island (30-A) side of Choctawhatchee Bay, near Topsail Hill Preserve State Park. Its habitat should track its larger neighbors — marsh grass, some oyster structure, and a modest interior — but there is less basis to speak confidently about it as a standalone fishery. It is best treated as a bonus stop on a Mack and Hewett Bayou trip rather than a primary destination.
buck.todaysCall: Buck Bayou makes the most sense today as a quick exploratory stop bolted onto a Mack-Hewett run — don't plan your day around it, but if you're already in the neighborhood and have time before the pre-4 PM storm window, a 20-minute poke inside is low-risk. The same approach that works at Mack and Hewett applies here: oyster edges and grass margins on the outgoing tide before the 10:15 AM low, with a slow presentation in slightly stained water. Light WSW winds won't impact this protected interior. Given the limited fishing history here, keep expectations flexible and let the water tell you whether fish are present before investing significant time.
